114681.etyen:
From fredag (“Friday”) + taco (“taco”), with linking -s- (“interfix”), literally “Friday taco”, referring to taco eaten as a regular Friday-evening meal. The first element, fredag (“Friday”), is inherited from Old Norse frjádagr (“Friday”), in which the first element represents the name of Frigg or Freyja, modelled on Latin dies Veneris (“day of Venus”). The second element, taco, is borrowed from Spanish taco (“taco”); the food term's deeper origin is uncertain, though it is often connected with the Spanish sense “plug, wad”. The compound is first attested before 2011.
Compare the equivalent S

6905.etyen:
Inherited from Middle Norwegian boltr (“bolt”), itself borrowed from Middle Low German bolte (“bolt”), from Old Saxon bolt (“bolt”), from Proto-West Germanic *bolt (“bolt”), from Proto-Germanic *bultaz (“bolt”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeld- (“to knock, strike”).
Compare Old Norse boltr (“bolt, bundle”), Swedish bult and German Bolzen (“bolt”). / Origin uncertain. The sense “story, tall tale” probably arose through sound association with dialectal bolte (“to boast”), possibly also influenced by the expression slå en plate (“to tell an invented story”). The boasting and tall-tale senses are recorded by Ivar Aasen in the 19th century. The person senses appear to be secondary; compare bult (“rough, noisy person”).
The formally similar person-forming element -bolt, as in drukkenbolt (“drunkard”), is etymologically separate, being borrowed from German -bold. / Borrowed from Middle Low German bolte (“bolt”), probably the same word as Etymology 1 and probably related to bylt (“bundle”). / Same historical word as Etymology 1, with a separate dialectal semantic development. Compare German Bolzen (“bolt; penis”). The semantic development to the animal senses is unclear.

1001465.etyen:
Internationalism, borrowed from Ancient Greek Χάρων (Khárōn, “Kharon, ferryman of the underworld”). The origin of the Ancient Greek name is uncertain. It has traditionally been associated with χάρων (khárōn, “fierce-eyed, bright-eyed”), a poetic form of χαρωπός (kharōpós, “fierce-eyed, bright-eyed”), but the connection is uncertain.
Compare the parallel learned and historically related forms Finnish Kharon, Hungarian Kharón, German Charon, Dutch Charon, French Charon, English Charon, Latin Charōn, and Modern Greek Greek Χάρων (Cháron) and Χάρος (Cháros).
